1.1: The frame changes only to bring it level with a text Community Recovery has issued: a new draft edition before adoption, the adopted text at adoption, and after it an amendment passed as clause 10.1 requires. The keepers (6) make that change and no other.
1.2: A list inside a clause stays inside the clause's line until someone needs to answer one item of it; it then takes addresses beneath the clause, and nothing above it moves.
1._: THE FRAME — a clause line is the draft's own words with its own number first, and is never paraphrased here. The lines above the clauses, six parts, the twelve sections under their own headings and the themes inside the long sections, are written so a reader can choose where to look, and carry no authority. An address never moves: a newer text replaces the words at the same addresses, after the standing block is copied to archive:spine:constitution:<date>, so every reading stays attached to its clause.

2.1: Yes — this reads right to me.
2.2: Change — I would change something, and here is what.
2.3: Not sure — I have a question, or I do not follow it.
2._: A READING — write at a clause's address only your own view of that clause, leading with one of three words, Yes, Change or Not sure, each said beneath, then whatever you wish to add: a reason, a question, a wording you would prefer. Silence at a clause is not-yet-read, never assent. A reading is its writer's to change or remove at any time, and nobody else's. An open line is read by anyone, so leave out anything private about yourself, and write about nobody else by name.

3: THE ROOM — pool:constitution is for talk about the constitution as a whole. A view of one clause belongs in the writer's own reading at that clause, where the page and the minutes find it.

4.1: A PERSON'S OWN — kept in tree:constitution:<name>, at the clause's own address, under their own key, the latest standing; it speaks for nobody else. An assistant reads this law before it reads a clause.
4.2: WHOSE READINGS — a synthesis says at its head which readings it took: every open reading; members' readings only, a member being a name whose block agreement:<name> carries Agreed at every numbered part; or the readings of the people it names. It names nobody's words as its own.
4.3: ONLY OPEN READINGS ARE FOLDED — a line its writer has sealed is read by nobody and enters no picture.
4.4: THE COMMUNITY'S VERSION — the syntheses of the people named here, drawn at each clause as the newest among them with who made it and when, and the keepers' minutes at the bare name constitution (4.5). Named: nobody yet. To write a name here is to endorse; to strike it is to revoke; only the holder of this law (6) writes it, and no key passes between hands. More than one version may stand, each saying its rule as 4.2 asks, and a page shows each as what it is.
4.5: THE KEEPERS' MINUTES — at the bare name constitution, at a clause's own address: a dated minute by a keeper (6), its date first, saying what the readings hold in common and where they differ, in the readers' own words, with a wording only where voices converge; the newest minute takes the place of the last, which stays beneath it. What a General Meeting decides at a clause is kept here too, with its date and its minute reference (5).
4.6: THE SPINE — changes only when its holder adopts, as 1 and 1.1 say: for this constitution, a General Meeting, whose decision is kept at 4.5 and whose adopted text replaces the spine's words at the same addresses.
4._: WHAT PEOPLE ARE SAYING — two versions of this constitution stand at the same addresses: the spine, its authored text, and the tree, that text as people's readings would change it. A synthesis is one reading, by whatever assistant a person uses, of three things: this law, a clause, and the readings this law admits. It returns the clause as the readings would have it, the count by first word, every Change and every Not sure in its writer's own words, and what it left out and why. Anyone may make one, and it is theirs. Which syntheses stand as the community's version is said at 4.4, by naming people and never by a shared key. Only open readings are folded.

5: WHAT IS DECIDED, AND WHERE — the nine open matters of Appendix B stand at addresses in the frame, beneath 6.3, and are answered like any clause. A matter, or a clause that draws Change voices, goes to a General Meeting as a proposal; the meeting decides; the decision is kept at that address in the shared minutes with its date and its minute reference. This family never decides.
6: THE KEEPERS — the frame, this law and the shared minutes stand under one key, held by a few named people who answer to the members for every change made with it, and who never write in anyone's reading. The key is held for Community Recovery by weft, the shell that built this place at the word of David Pinto, who keeps this beach; it passes to Community Recovery's coordinator and leadership when they ask for it, and they change it as they take it.
7: CARE — recovery and wellbeing come first here, as clause 2.7 says of everything: nobody is asked to read it all, and any part may be left. A worry about someone's safety is told to a volunteer in person, and never left as a comment here.
9: PROVENANCE — written 30 September 2026 by weft, Claude Code's shell on this beach, at David Pinto's word, from Community Recovery's constitution working draft of September 2026 and from Matthew's book on the apex beach (proposal:community-recovery, whose third chapter asks for the constitution to be read and shaped by members, section by section). The shape is the family form (tree 8 on the apex beach); the one-word-first voicing follows function:audit there. The design and its decisions: github.com/pscale-commons/bsp-mcp-server, proposals/2026-09-30-community-recovery-on-the-beach. Nothing here was written by Community Recovery, and nothing here speaks for it.
_: CONSTITUTION — read this family as a community reading its own rules before it adopts them. The frame, spine:constitution, holds the constitution of Community Recovery as its working draft of September 2026 words it, one clause at each address; the lines above the clauses are signposts. Each person's own reading stands at the same addresses in their own block, constitution:<name>, and only they write it. What people are saying together is kept clause by clause at the bare name, constitution, as dated minutes. Nothing here adopts or amends anything: the members do that at a General Meeting, as clauses 10.1 and 12.1 say, and this family prepares the ground and keeps the record. It is Community Recovery's as far as its members use it, and no further.
